observations: Production server-rendered websites exhibit extremely high URL-level leakage: Wikipedia 91.2%, GitHub 77.8%, MDN 92.0% of transitions have action.target_href == state_after.url. This means clicking a link on these sites almost always navigates to the exact URL encoded in the href, which is expected behavior for server-rendered sites where links encode full destination URLs.

After non-leakage filtering, the remaining transitions are extremely sparse: Wikipedia 8 NL (from 91 raw), GitHub 4 NL (from 18 raw), MDN 2 NL (from 25 raw). All three sites fall far below the 50 NL threshold required by the frozen decision rule (C7).

Wikipedia's 8 NL transitions have 6 unique URLs and 6 unique title-URL pairs, resulting in PMI = 0.0 bits because each (state, action, next_state) triple is unique (singleton SA pairs). The Laplace-smoothed PMI formula gives log2(1/N / (1 * 1)) = 0 when count_sas_next = 1 and distinct_actions_s = distinct_next_s = N.

Wikipedia H(S_next | URL) = 0.647 bits on all 91 transitions (exceeding 0.2 threshold), but H(S_next | URL) = 0.0 on the 8 NL transitions only. The ceiling exists on the full dataset but vanishes in the NL subset because the NL transitions are the 'surprising' ones where navigation didn't follow the expected path.

The positive control (8-state linear SPA with unique deterministic titles) passes strongly: BC PMI = 1.841 bits, permutation p = 0.001, determinism accuracy = 1.0. The PMI pipeline correctly detects known deterministic structure.
Title variation check passes on all 3 sites (>= 2 unique titles), but this is uninformative because the NL subsets are too small for PMI analysis.

Playwright browser automation encountered persistent EPIPE errors in the CI environment, limiting data collection to small batches (5-15 trajectories per session) with crashes on context close. Despite this, sufficient raw transitions were collected to diagnose the fundamental problem: high URL-level leakage on production server-rendered sites.

The 91% leakage rate on Wikipedia is a structural property of server-rendered sites: <a href="/wiki/Article"> links encode the full destination URL in the href attribute, so action.target_href == state_after.url by construction for link navigation. Only button clicks, form submissions, and JavaScript-triggered navigation can produce non-leakage transitions.
validity_notes: MEASUREMENT_INVALID because C7 (>= 50 NL per site on >= 2/3 sites) fails: 0/3 sites meet threshold. This is not a scientific negative but an infrastructure/data-sufficiency failure.

The high leakage rate (78-92%) on production server-rendered sites is a structural property, not a measurement artifact. Link hrefs on these sites encode full destination URLs, making leakage the expected outcome for link-based navigation.
The PMI pipeline is validated by the positive control (BC PMI = 1.841, p = 0.001) but cannot be meaningfully applied to the NL subsets because they are too small (< 10 transitions per site).

Playwright EPIPE errors in the CI environment limited data collection but did not cause the MEASUREMENT_INVALID outcome. Even with unlimited collection time, the 78-92% leakage rate means collecting 50 NL transitions would require 250-450 raw transitions per site (50 / (1 - leakage_rate)), which is achievable but was not reached in this run.

The frozen decision rule's C8 (H(S_next|URL,H_K=3) > 0.2) passes for Wikipedia on ALL transitions (H = 0.647) but fails on NL only (H = 0.0). This reveals that the NL subset is the problematic regime for PMI analysis.

Server-rendered sites (Wikipedia, MDN, GitHub) are not SPAs. The C-WEB-DYNAMICS claim concerns interactive Web transformations broadly, but this experiment specifically tested server-rendered sites. SPA-form-heavy sites may exhibit lower leakage rates and more title-dependent navigation.
unresolved: Whether production SPAs (hash-based routing, client-side rendering) exhibit lower URL-level leakage rates than server-rendered sites, enabling more NL transitions for PMI analysis.
Whether the non-leakage fraction can be increased by targeting form submissions, button clicks, and JavaScript-triggered navigation instead of link clicks.
Whether the 50 NL threshold is achievable on production sites with browser automation, given the structural leakage property of server-rendered link navigation.
Whether the title-aware PMI pipeline can detect predictive structure on the small NL subsets if a more powerful estimator is used (e.g., Bayesian PMI, trajectory-level mutual information).

Whether the synthetic-to-real gap can be bridged by targeting SPA sites where URL routing is ambiguous (multiple states share the same URL path but differ in client-side state), reducing the leakage rate.
